Tomato_Bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.summary: Small dark leaf spots, often with yellow halos, that can also mark stems and fruit.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.overview: Bacterial spot is a group of related bacterial diseases that can affect tomato leaves, stems, petioles and fruit. Early symptoms can look like several fungal leaf-spot diseases, so a photo is only a starting point.

causes.pathogen: Several Xanthomonas species can cause bacterial spot.
causes.conditions: Warm, humid weather, frequent rain or overhead irrigation, wet foliage and contaminated seed, transplants, tools or plant debris favor infection.

symptoms.leaves: Small brown or dark circular spots may have a yellow halo. Centers can fall out and leave a shot-hole appearance; concentric rings are less typical than in early blight.
symptoms.stems: Small dark spots or blotchy lesions may appear on stems and petioles.
symptoms.fruit: Green or ripe fruit can develop raised brown, corky or scabby spots, sometimes with a pale halo.

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.duration: New lesions can appear quickly during warm, wet periods and the disease may continue through the season while foliage stays wet.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.effects: Severe infection can reduce leaf area, expose fruit to sun injury and make fruit less marketable. Yield impact depends on timing, cultivar and weather.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.spread: Rain splash, overhead irrigation, hands, tools, infected seed or transplants and crop debris can move the bacteria between plants.
prevention: Start with reputable, disease-free seed and transplants.
Water at the soil line and improve spacing and airflow so leaves dry quickly.
Sanitize tools and remove or bury crop debris after harvest.
Rotate away from tomato and pepper when practical.
management: Scout lower leaves and remove badly affected tissue without removing most of the canopy at once.
Avoid working among plants while foliage is wet.
Ask a local extension or agricultural officer about locally registered products and resistance concerns; follow every label and harvest interval.
Get a laboratory diagnosis if the distinction from early blight, Septoria or target spot will change management.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.symptom_snapshot: Tiny dark spots and possible yellow halos; usually no clear concentric rings.

Tomato_Early_blight.name: Early blight
Tomato_Early_blight.summary: Brown target-like spots that often begin on older, lower leaves and move upward.
Tomato_Early_blight.overview: Early blight is a common tomato disease caused by Alternaria fungi. It often starts in older foliage near the soil and may affect leaves, stems and fruit.

causes.pathogen: Alternaria solani and related Alternaria species are associated with early blight.
causes.conditions: Warm temperatures, leaf wetness, heavy dew, rain splash and infected crop debris create favorable conditions.

symptoms.leaves: Round to irregular brown spots enlarge into target-like concentric rings, often with yellow tissue around them. Older leaves may yellow, dry and drop.
symptoms.stems: Dark, dry lesions can form on stems, especially near the soil line or on older branches.
symptoms.fruit: Dark, leathery spots with raised rings may develop near the stem end of fruit.

Tomato_Early_blight.duration: The disease can repeat in cycles during a warm, wet growing season; new spots may develop within days when foliage remains wet.
Tomato_Early_blight.effects: Defoliation can reduce plant vigor and expose fruit to sunscald. Fruit damage and yield loss are more likely when infection is early or severe.
Tomato_Early_blight.spread: Spores move from infected debris and weeds by rain splash, wind, handling and equipment. The pathogen can survive between crops in residue.
prevention: Use mulch to reduce soil splash and keep lower leaves away from wet soil.
Stake or cage plants, prune carefully and provide good air movement.
Water at the base in the morning and remove diseased residue after harvest.
Rotate tomato and other susceptible solanaceous crops when practical.
management: Remove the most affected leaves early while preserving enough healthy foliage for the plant.
Avoid overhead irrigation and disinfect tools between plants.
Ask a local agricultural professional about resistant varieties and registered fungicide options; products are often preventive and must be used by label.
Compare target-like rings with the smaller spots of Septoria and bacterial spot before deciding on treatment.
Tomato_Early_blight.symptom_snapshot: Brown spots with visible concentric rings, often beginning on lower leaves.

Tomato_Late_blight.name: Late blight
Tomato_Late_blight.summary: Large water-soaked brown blotches that can spread rapidly in cool, wet weather.
Tomato_Late_blight.overview: Late blight is caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans. It can affect leaves, stems and fruit and may progress quickly when conditions are cool and wet.

causes.pathogen: Phytophthora infestans, a fungal-like water mold.
causes.conditions: Cool, damp weather, prolonged leaf wetness, rain, high humidity and infected plant material favor spread.

symptoms.leaves: Large irregular water-soaked or olive-to-brown blotches can cross leaf veins. In humid conditions, pale growth may appear at lesion edges or undersides.
symptoms.stems: Firm dark brown lesions can expand along stems and petioles, causing rapid wilt or collapse.
symptoms.fruit: Firm dark brown spots can cover large areas of fruit and may become soft after secondary organisms enter.

Tomato_Late_blight.duration: Under favorable weather, new infections and spread can be very fast, sometimes over only a few days.
Tomato_Late_blight.effects: Severe outbreaks can destroy foliage and fruit and may cause major crop loss. Urgent confirmation is sensible when symptoms spread quickly.
Tomato_Late_blight.spread: Windborne spores, rain splash, infected transplants, volunteer plants and infected potato or tomato material can spread the pathogen.
prevention: Inspect transplants and avoid bringing suspect material into a crop.
Improve airflow, avoid wet foliage and remove volunteer potato or tomato plants.
Monitor local disease alerts during cool, wet weather.
Remove infected debris responsibly and do not save seed or fruit from suspect plants.
management: Separate suspect plants and seek prompt confirmation from a local plant clinic or agricultural officer.
Do not rely on a photograph alone when the disease is spreading rapidly.
Ask about locally registered protective products and resistance management; follow the label exactly.
Do not compost heavily infected material unless the local guidance says the process is suitable.
Tomato_Late_blight.symptom_snapshot: Large irregular blotches with a water-soaked look and unusually rapid spread.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.name: Leaf mold
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.summary: Yellow-green upper-leaf patches with olive, velvety growth on the underside in humid shelters.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.overview: Tomato leaf mold is most often a greenhouse or high-tunnel problem. It is caused by Passalora fulva and is strongly associated with high humidity and limited airflow.

causes.pathogen: Passalora fulva, formerly called Fulvia fulva or Cladosporium fulvum.
causes.conditions: Relative humidity above about 85%, condensation, crowded plants and poor ventilation encourage disease.

symptoms.leaves: Pale yellow or green spots appear on the upper surface; olive-green to brown velvety growth may appear directly beneath them.
symptoms.stems: Stem symptoms are less prominent but darkened areas may occur on affected plant tissue.
symptoms.fruit: Blossoms may darken and fall. Fruit can develop a smooth black area near the stem that becomes sunken and leathery.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.duration: New spore cycles can form in roughly one to two weeks when humidity remains high, allowing repeated spread in protected culture.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.effects: Severe leaf loss reduces photosynthesis and can reduce yield; blossom and fruit infection can add direct losses.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.spread: Spores move by air currents, water, tools, workers and possibly insects. Seed and plant debris can introduce or carry the pathogen.
prevention: Ventilate greenhouses and tunnels and reduce condensation overnight.
Space, stake and prune plants to improve airflow without excessive leaf removal.
Water at the base and sanitize tools, supports and work surfaces.
Remove crop residue and consider locally suitable resistant varieties.
management: Reduce humidity and remove the most affected leaves carefully.
Increase air movement and keep foliage dry; cultural changes are central to control.
Ask a local professional about registered products for protected culture and follow greenhouse restrictions on the label.
Confirm the underside of the leaf because several problems can create yellow upper-surface patches.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.symptom_snapshot: Yellow upper patches paired with olive velvety growth underneath, especially in humid shelters.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Many small spots with dark margins, pale centers and tiny dark specks, usually on lower leaves.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.overview: Septoria leaf spot is caused by Septoria lycopersici. It mainly damages foliage and can defoliate a plant when wet weather allows repeated infection.

causes.pathogen: Septoria lycopersici, a fungus that survives in infected debris and can be carried on seed or transplants.
causes.conditions: High humidity, leaf wetness, rain splash and moderate temperatures favor infection.

symptoms.leaves: Small circular spots have a dark border and tan or gray center. Tiny black fruiting bodies may appear in the center as spots mature.
symptoms.stems: Spots can occur on stems, petioles and sepals, although leaves are usually the most noticeable site.
symptoms.fruit: Fruit is rarely affected directly; defoliation can expose fruit to sunscald.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.duration: The disease can produce repeated infection cycles through a wet season, often moving from lower leaves upward.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.effects: Heavy defoliation weakens the plant and exposes fruit. Early, widespread infection can reduce crop quality and yield.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.spread: Spores spread by rain or irrigation splash, tools, hands, insects and infected plant residue.
prevention: Use mulch to limit splash from soil and keep lower leaves dry.
Water at the plant base, provide airflow and avoid handling wet plants.
Remove infected leaves and residue, but do not strip more foliage than necessary.
Rotate crops and use clean seed or transplants.
management: Scout lower leaves and remove the first affected leaves when practical.
Sanitize tools and wash hands after handling suspect plants.
Ask a local agricultural officer about resistant varieties and registered protectants; follow labels and harvest intervals.
Compare the small pale-centered spots with the rings of early blight and the halos of bacterial spot.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.symptom_snapshot: Numerous small pale-centered spots with dark edges and tiny black specks.

Tomato_Spider_mites.name: Spider mites
Tomato_Spider_mites.summary: Fine stippling, yellowing and webbing caused by tiny mites, often during hot, dry conditions.
Tomato_Spider_mites.overview: Spider mites are very small plant-feeding pests rather than a disease. They often hide on leaf undersides and can be difficult to confirm from a single image.

causes.pathogen: Common tomato problems involve two-spotted or related spider mites in the Tetranychus group.
causes.conditions: Hot, dry weather, dusty conditions, plant stress and loss of natural enemies can favor population growth.

symptoms.leaves: Fine pale stippling develops into yellow or bronze foliage. Turn leaves over to look for tiny moving mites, cast skins or fine webbing.
symptoms.stems: Heavy infestations may leave webbing around petioles and growing tips.
symptoms.fruit: Fruit is usually affected indirectly through loss of healthy foliage and plant vigor rather than by distinctive fruit lesions.

Tomato_Spider_mites.duration: Several generations can develop quickly in hot conditions, so damage may increase noticeably over days to weeks.
Tomato_Spider_mites.effects: Feeding reduces photosynthesis, weakens plants and can cause early leaf drop. Severe pressure can reduce fruit size and yield.
Tomato_Spider_mites.spread: Mites can move by wind, people, tools, plant material and contact between touching leaves.
prevention: Reduce plant stress and wash dusty foliage gently when appropriate.
Inspect leaf undersides and new plants before bringing them near the crop.
Protect beneficial predators and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides.
Keep weeds and volunteer plants monitored around the crop.
management: Confirm mites or webbing on leaf undersides before choosing a response.
Use a strong but plant-safe water spray where appropriate and repeat monitoring.
Ask a local professional about registered miticides, insecticidal soaps or oils for the crop and conditions; follow labels and test for plant sensitivity.
Avoid assuming every yellow or stippled leaf is a mite problem.
Tomato_Spider_mites.symptom_snapshot: Fine pale stippling, underside webbing and tiny moving pests in hot, dry conditions.

Tomato_Target_Spot.name: Target spot
Tomato_Target_Spot.summary: Brown leaf and fruit lesions that may develop concentric rings and expand in warm, wet weather.
Tomato_Target_Spot.overview: Target spot is a fungal disease that can affect tomato leaves, stems and fruit. It may resemble early blight or bacterial spot, especially in early stages.

causes.pathogen: Target spot is commonly associated with Corynespora cassiicola.
causes.conditions: Warm temperatures, high humidity, extended leaf wetness, dense canopies and rain or overhead irrigation favor disease.

symptoms.leaves: Small brown spots can enlarge and form tan or dark concentric rings; surrounding tissue may yellow and spots may merge.
symptoms.stems: Dark elongated lesions may form on stems and petioles.
symptoms.fruit: Fruit can develop sunken, dark lesions, often near the shoulder or stem area, sometimes with ringed patterns.

Tomato_Target_Spot.duration: Disease cycles repeat during warm, humid weather and can move up the canopy when foliage remains wet.
Tomato_Target_Spot.effects: Leaf loss reduces photosynthesis and fruit lesions reduce marketability. Severity varies with cultivar, environment and timing.
Tomato_Target_Spot.spread: Spores move by wind, rain splash, irrigation, tools, workers and infected plant residue.
prevention: Use clean transplants, good spacing and trellising to improve airflow.
Water at the base and avoid working the crop while leaves are wet.
Remove crop residue and manage volunteer plants and weeds.
Rotate crops when practical and monitor lower leaves early.
management: Remove severely affected tissue while keeping enough healthy foliage for the plant.
Reduce leaf wetness and sanitize tools between plants.
Ask a local agricultural professional about registered fungicides and resistance management; follow the product label.
Seek confirmation if target spot, early blight or bacterial spot would lead to different decisions.
Tomato_Target_Spot.symptom_snapshot: Brown lesions with possible concentric rings on leaves, stems or fruit.

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: Leaf curling, yellowing and stunting commonly associated with whitefly-transmitted virus infection.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.overview: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus can cause severe growth and yield problems. Visual symptoms overlap with other viruses, herbicide injury and nutrient or environmental stress, so confirmation may require a plant clinic or lab.

causes.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus and related begomoviruses; the exact virus depends on region.
causes.conditions: Whiteflies can acquire and spread the virus. Warm conditions and infected plants or weeds can sustain the disease cycle.

symptoms.leaves: Young leaves may curl upward, become smaller, yellow between veins and show a cupped or stiff appearance.
symptoms.stems: Plants may be shortened, branched or stunted; young growth can remain crowded and pale.
symptoms.fruit: Flower drop, poor fruit set and small or uneven fruit can follow early infection.

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.duration: An infected plant does not recover from virus infection; symptoms and yield effects continue as new growth develops.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.effects: Early infection can severely stunt plants, reduce flowering and reduce fruit number or size.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.spread: Whiteflies transmit the virus from infected plants. Transplants, weeds and volunteer plants can help introduce or maintain infection.
prevention: Use healthy transplants and monitor for whiteflies on leaf undersides.
Remove heavily symptomatic plants when local guidance recommends it and manage weed hosts.
Use regionally appropriate resistant varieties where available.
Use screens or exclusion methods in protected culture when suitable.
management: Treat the result as a suspicion, not a confirmed virus diagnosis.
Control the vector and remove infected sources according to local extension guidance.
Ask an agricultural officer about locally registered whitefly management options; follow labels and protect beneficial insects.
Submit a sample for laboratory confirmation when the crop value or management decision warrants it.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptom_snapshot: New leaves curl and yellow while the plant becomes shortened or stunted.

Tomato_healthy.name: Healthy leaf
Tomato_healthy.summary: A reference class for leaves without strong visual evidence of the labeled diseases.
Tomato_healthy.overview: The healthy class means the model found the uploaded image most similar to healthy examples in its training data. It is not a guarantee that the whole plant is disease-free.

causes.pathogen: No disease pathogen is implied by this reference class.
causes.conditions: Healthy leaves usually have even green color, normal shape and no strong pattern of lesions, webbing or distortion.

symptoms.leaves: Even green color, intact tissue and normal leaf shape are common reference features.
symptoms.stems: Stems should be firm and free of suspicious lesions or collapse.
symptoms.fruit: A leaf photo cannot assess fruit condition; inspect flowers and fruit separately.

Tomato_healthy.duration: Plant health can change after the photo. Continue scouting during the growing season.
Tomato_healthy.effects: A healthy-looking leaf supports growth, but hidden, early or non-leaf problems may still be present.
Tomato_healthy.spread: No spread is implied by this class. Continue hygiene and monitoring practices.
prevention: Maintain appropriate spacing, airflow, irrigation and nutrition.
Scout both upper and lower leaf surfaces and inspect stems and fruit.
Remove plant debris and sanitize tools between suspect plants.
Use local integrated pest-management guidance when conditions change.
management: No treatment is suggested by the healthy reference class.
If the plant looks different in person, take several clear photos and seek local advice.
Do not use a healthy model result to override obvious field symptoms.
Tomato_healthy.symptom_snapshot: Even green tissue and normal shape in the photographed leaf; inspect the whole plant too.

Tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus
Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: Mottled light and dark green leaves, distortion and possible plant stunting caused by a virus.
Tomato_mosaic_virus.overview: Tomato mosaic virus is one of several viruses that can affect tomatoes. Visual patterns overlap between viruses and other stresses, so a photo cannot confirm the exact virus.

causes.pathogen: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a tobamovirus; related viruses can cause similar symptoms.
causes.conditions: The virus can persist on contaminated plant material and spread through sap, tools, hands, seed and contact between plants.

symptoms.leaves: Light and dark green mosaic, mottling, curling, narrowing or distorted leaflets may appear.
symptoms.stems: Growth may be shortened or irregular; symptoms can vary with cultivar, plant age and environmental conditions.
symptoms.fruit: Fruit may ripen unevenly, be smaller or show internal or surface discoloration in some infections.

Tomato_mosaic_virus.duration: Virus-infected plants do not recover, and symptoms can remain or intensify as new growth develops.
Tomato_mosaic_virus.effects: Early infection can reduce vigor, fruit number and fruit size. Effects vary by strain, cultivar and plant age.
Tomato_mosaic_virus.spread: Sap on hands, tools, stakes, clothing, plant contact, infected seed and crop residue can spread tobamoviruses.
prevention: Use clean seed and healthy transplants from reputable sources.
Wash hands and sanitize tools after handling suspect plants.
Avoid tobacco products around tomato work because tobamoviruses can be carried in plant residue.
Remove volunteer plants and manage crop debris responsibly.
management: Treat visual identification as provisional and seek lab confirmation when important.
Remove confirmed infected plants where local guidance recommends it to reduce sources.
Do not save seed from suspect plants and avoid propagating cuttings from them.
Ask a local agricultural officer about resistant varieties and sanitation practices.
Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptom_snapshot: Mottled light and dark green leaves with possible curling, distortion or stunting.
